definition: Mercenary means motivated entirely by money or personal gain — willing to do, drop, or switch anything if it pays.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mercenary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mercenary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her tell-all book about the scandal struck reviewers as mercenary — rushed to print for the trial's opening day and padded to justify the price.
Opportunistic is milder than mercenary: the opportunist grabs advantages as they float past, while the mercenary has gone further — pay has become the whole compass.
Venal is darker than mercenary: mercenary loyalty merely follows the highest bidder, but venality puts duties and offices themselves up for sale — the judge's ruling, the inspector's signature.
Greedy means wanting more and more of something than you need — food, money, attention; it measures the appetite's size, while mercenary is about what steers the choices: pay, and pay alone.
Venal means open to bribery — a venal official sells the powers of an office; mercenary conduct needn't be corrupt at all, just priced: the mercenary consultant works for whoever writes the check.
Self-serving means arranged to benefit oneself in whatever currency — credit, comfort, advancement; mercenary names the money version specifically.

Mercenary is an accusation about motive: not 'did money change hands' but 'was money the reason.' The word began as a noun — a mercenarius was a soldier fighting for wages rather than for a country — and the adjective keeps that chill: allegiance for hire.
Mercenary is a verdict on motive, so save it for cases where the money truly did the steering — charging for work is not mercenary; abandoning a loyalty for a better fee is.
As a noun it still means a soldier for hire, and the adjective borrows that figure's chill: whatever it modifies, somewhere a flag has been traded for a paycheck.
